groups.label: Plato's Legal and State Works
groups.summary: Commentary examines Plato's treatment of law, medicine, and governance across works, contrasting the idealism of the Republic with the practical legalism of the Laws and the rule-of-law inquiries of the Statesman.
groups.rationale: These entries are contiguous commentary nodes focusing directly on Plato's own texts and internal evolution regarding law, statecraft, and governance.

groups.label: Platonic Ideal Commonwealths
groups.summary: Historical thinkers from Cicero and Augustine to Dante, More, and Campanella adapt or contrast Platonic political visions, creating diverse conceptions of universal empires, heavenly cities, and communistic commonwealths.
groups.rationale: This sequence of commentary traces the reception and adaptation of Plato's ideal commonwealth across later classical, medieval, and Renaissance political thinkers.

groups.label: Book I: Justice and Ruling
groups.summary: Cephalus links age, wealth, and moral peace of mind, prompting Socrates to refute simple accounts of justice as repaying debts and to demonstrate that rulers err when defining their own advantage.
groups.rationale: These entries form the opening dialogue of Book I, transitioning from Cephalus's conventional views of justice to Socrates' refutations of debt and ruler infallibility.

groups.label: Socrates' Aporia in Book I
groups.summary: At the conclusion of Book I, both an editorial sidenote and Socrates' own remarks describe his dissatisfaction and aporia after wandering into side inquiries without defining justice itself.
groups.rationale: Both items document the exact moment of aporia and self-blame that concludes the Book I inquiry.

groups.label: Adeimantus' Challenge to Socrates
groups.summary: Adeimantus critiques the conventional defense of justice for worldly and divine gain, challenging Socrates to explain what justice and injustice do intrinsically within the soul.
groups.rationale: A cohesive two-part speech by Adeimantus at the start of Book II demanding an intrinsic defense of justice.

groups.label: Education of the Guardians
groups.summary: Socrates outlines the character and curriculum of the guardians, balancing spiritedness with gentleness and censoring frightening depictions of Hades to instill courage against death.
groups.rationale: These contiguous Book II and III dialogue entries establish the temperamental traits and poetic censorship required to train courageous guardians.
